It outlines methods for 3D text encoding, leveraging TEI, especially using the EpiDoc schema and extending it for 3D applications. The paper emphasizes the advantage of adopting the genetic edition–like markup using , to document spatial data, particularly 3D coordinates, to fully represent text in 3D space. The paper contributes to the discussion on encoding textual data in 3D environments, proposing adjustments to existing schemas to accommodate 3D information and highlighting the need for further development in this emerging field.
venue_name: Journal of the Text Encoding Initiative, Vol 18 (2026)

title: L’enseignement critique des savoirs environnementaux en école d’agronomie : comment favoriser un tournant écologique sur le plan pédagogique et éducatif ?
abstract: Higher education and research teaching staff have been thinking about how to answer environmental and climate issues in their respective institutions and in their teaching approaches. This article looks at the scope and content of a pedagogical reform within the student curricula of an agronomy school in France. We begin by reviewing a number of initiatives undertaken in recent years in France. We then present our approach to analyze the literature and deduce ways in which we can take account of the challenges of bifurcation in our school. Interdisciplinarity and transdisciplinarity put into practice on the educational level in the name of the complexity of the issues at stake, the learning of critical thinking and the use of various types of didactics, are paths conducive to learning and putting environmental knowledge into context.

title: Connaître la nature. Dialogues à l’interface entre la Political Ecology et les Sciences and Technology Studies (introduction du livre)
abstract: This introduction to Knowing Nature (2011) examines and contributes to the theoretical foundations of political ecology, drawing on science studies perspectives. The text describes an approach to environmental issues in the social sciences, linking the production, circulation, and use of environmental knowledge. Additionally, this translation provides insight into the scientific issues that were addressed in the United States during the 2010s.

title: Parents LGBTQ+ au Québec : expériences de microaffirmations et de microagressions au sein des milieux éducatifs fréquentés par leurs enfants.
abstract: Research framework: Despite socio-legal advances promoting the recognition and protection of LGBTQ+ families in Quebec, persistent heterocisnormativity risks creating more subtle forms of stigmatization, particularly in childcare services and school environments frequented by children.Objectives: This study examines the dynamics of inclusion and exclusion experienced by LGBTQ+ parents in their children’s educational settings through the concepts of microaffirmations (MAF) and microaggressions (MAG). It also analyzes how specific characteristics, such as age, sexual orientation and gender identity, may influence these experiences.Methodology: Exploratory factor analyses and latent class analyses were carried out using data from 428 parents who responded to an online questionnaire as part of the Understanding Inclusion and Exclusion of LGBTQ People project.Results: Three latent classes presented low, moderate or frequent exposure to MAF and MAG. A dominant MAF class included parents who mainly benefited from microaffirmations, while a dominant MAG class reported frequent experiences of microaggressions. Parents in marginalized or precarious situations were more likely to belong to classes reporting fewer MAF (limited exposure, dominant MAG), while the dominant MAF class included more monosexual, cisgender individuals with an annual income above $100,000.Conclusions: The majority of LGBTQ+ parents in the sample were exposed, to varying degrees, to MAF and MAG in the educational settings attended by their children. The coexistence of MAG and MAF observed serves as a reminder that the absence of explicit stigma does not guarantee the full inclusion of family diversity. Contribution: This study sheds new light on the experiences of LGBTQ+ parents in Quebec educational settings. It highlights the need to train educational staff on family diversity in order to foster a more inclusive environment. Recommendations are made for adapting education policies to the diverse realities of LGBTQ+ families.
publisher: Centre Urbanisation Culture Société (UCS) de l'INRS

title: Formation par la perturbation : effets sur les préoccupations et l’apprentissage collectif à partir de l’expérience vécue
abstract: This study analyses the effects of a perturbation-based simulation training programme, focusing on individual concerns and collective learning processes that emerge during the activity. Analysis of the experiences of three learners highlights the heterogeneity of these experiences and the differentiated effects of disruption on individual activity. These differences nevertheless foster collective adaptation through mutual adjustments and the mobilisation of socio-affective dimensions. Our results show that these localised effects are useful indicators allowing trainers to regulate learners’ activity during simulation. Furthermore, the study highlights the emergence of collective learning processes described in the literature (sharing, reflexivity, co-construction), and an original process, that of the protection of the collective, defined as the spontaneous response to an event threatening the continuity of collective activity. This process contributes to the reconfiguration of the activity and to the development of a collective awareness of the situation, which is conducive to adaptation in complex and uncertain contexts. These results highlight the value of perturbation simulation in enriching collective learning.
publisher: Association Recherche et Pratique sur les Activités

title: Former à soigner autrement ? Analyse didactique d’une démarche low‑tech de simulation en santé
abstract: In view of the growing contribution of healthcare systems to ecosystem degradation, training institutions are increasingly called upon to rethink their pedagogical practices, particularly in simulation-based education. This article examines the emergence of low-tech approaches in health simulation as an alternative to the dominant paradigm based on high technologization and realistic reproduction of clinical environments. Building on prior work addressing the ecological impact of healthcare systems and sustainability initiatives developed in certain simulation centers, the article identifies the core principles structuring a low-tech approach across four dimensions: usefulness, durability, accessibility, and appropriation. Through a case study illustrative of an institutional culture oriented toward sustainability, the analysis focuses on the activity of designing a wound simulation model, drawing on the theoretical contributions of professional didactics. The article concludes by framing simulation as a space for pedagogical and institutional experimentation, within which more frugal and sustainable forms of care-related activity can be envisioned.
publisher: Association Recherche et Pratique sur les Activités

title: Former à la gestion de crise par la simulation : réflexions à partir d’un modèle de l’activité d’adaptation pour gérer les risques dans différents types de situation de crise
abstract: Crisis management is a complex activity that involves numerous challenges, including during the activity of crisis units. Scientific literature still offers relatively few models to help us understand these challenges—models that might nonetheless provide a relevant foundation for developing the ability of operators to manage crisis situations. This article aims to address this limitation by combining two perspectives: the modeling of operator activity in crisis situations, and the design of simulation-based training. We first describe the foundations of the model, then present it in detail. The model subsequently allows us to formulate avenues for reflection on simulation-based training for risk management across various types of crisis situation. In concrete terms, it involves an articulation between general (adaptation, transformation, progression) and specific principles (unique to each type of crisis situation). This approach aims to enhance the relevance and effectiveness of simulations, thereby fostering the development of adaptative activity to manage risks in different types of crisis situation.
publisher: Association Recherche et Pratique sur les Activités

title: Entre approche critique et opérationnelle, quelle dialectique ? Retour sur le rôle d’agent intermédiaire de la géographie politique de l’énergie
abstract: This article explores the complex role of social science researchers acting as advisory partners and intermediary agent within European energy transition frameworks. Specifically, it examines the SIreNERGY project (Interreg Europe), which aims to foster Renewable Energy Sources (RES) in rural areas through the lenses of social acceptance and citizen participation. The research focuses on a central tension: how can political geography maintain its critical edge while being "enrolled" to provide operational tools for public policy practitioners?Research positioning and theoretical frameworkThe study is situated at the intersection of political geography, political ecology, and transition studies. Historically, geography has oscillated between being a “service to power” and a tool for radically criticizing the system. In the context of the climate crisis, the European Union increasingly requires citizen participation and social acceptance as prerequisites for energy projects. However, many researchers fear that these concepts are used superficially. Instead of giving real power to citizens, they sometimes simply serve to make people accept projects imposed from above (acceptance management). The authors of this article position themselves as intermediary agents. This position is not understood as a neutral, technical transfer, but as a political act of translation. Their goal is to translate complex theories (i.e. power inequalities, energy justice,…) into operational tools without diluting their critical substance.Methodology: embedded reflexivity and “tiny tools”The methodology relies on an embedded research posture, focused on participant observation. The empirical material consists of: (i) Two Holistic Diagnostics conducted across five EU regions (Spain/Basque Country, Sweden, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria) to map energy profiles and social perceptions; (ii) Two surveys, through common questionnaires tracking changes in partners’ perceptions; (iii)Collective workshops, using “tiny tools” – i.e. simplified analytical frameworks to encourage practitioners to reflect on their own power dynamics; (iv) Cartographic visualization translating qualitative social data into interactive maps to facilitate multi-stakeholder dialogue.Main resultsThe findings of this research highlight the challenges faced by political geography when it is “enrolled” into energy transition programs. By acting as intermediaries, this article identified three main types of results: (i) Methodological reduction and instrumentalization: To make critical concepts accessible, researchers provided clear frameworks, but risked reducing the depth of the critique. This led to a paradox: while tools helped partners move beyond simple information-sharing, many still viewed “social mentality” or “lack of trust” as the primary barriers, rather than questioning the socio-political structures of the projects themselve. (ii) The balance between objectivity and prescription: The researcher’s role oscillated between being a neutral observer (objectification) and an active advisor (prescription). Because citizen participation remained marginal, the researchers stepped out of their neutral posture to promote the “Energy Community” model. However, this created a gap between the EU’s “ideal” model and local realities where such initiatives were misunderstood or absent. (3) The structural limits of “enrolled” geography: The study identifies spatial limits (the gap between European literature and local histories, such as the suspicion toward cooperatives in post-communist contexts); temporal limits (the short timeframe of Interreg prevents long-term follow-up of how tools are used); and action limits (being “close to power” favors energy deployment over challenging transition goals).

title: Une transition énergétique « géopolitique » ? Le rôle de la Commission européenne dans la réponse européenne à la crise de l’énergie (2021-2023)
abstract: The aim of this article is to examine the European Commission's political action during the energy crisis (2021–2023) by focusing on conflicts between actors regarding the appropriate geographical scale for responding to this crisis. While the first few months of the crisis may have encouraged some EU member states to prioritise national energy policies, the European Commission quickly intervened to use the crisis as a new milestone for EU institutions' political action in the field of energy through the REPowerEU plan. The article questions this position taken by the Commission, both in its official statements and in the instruments proposed in 2022, with the aim of examining the influence of the crisis in the ongoing implementation of European energy governance as part of the European Union’s policy action to achieve infrastructure integration, market liberalisation and energy transition in line with the EU's climate objectives. This article contributes to the field of European integration studies by examining the instruments and discourse of the REPowerEU plan as a new phase in the integration of national energy policies at the EU level. The literature on European integration offers multiple explanations for this process. Some scholars, adopting a neo-functionalist perspective, highlight the expansion of EU institutional powers (Maltby, 2013), while others, from an intergovernmental perspective, emphasize the persistent influence of Member States (Thaler, 2016). Although the progressive integration of energy policies at the EU level is widely acknowledged, it occurs in a context where the division of competences between EU institutions and Member States remains unstable (Szulecki & Westphal, 2018 ; Herranz-Surrallés et al., 2020) and primarily manifests through evaluation and oversight mechanisms within EU institutions (Knodt & Schoenefeld, 2020; Bocquillon & Maltby, 2020). Consequently, energy integration at the EU level is a hybrid process, shaped by consensus-building between Member States and EU institutions, where competing rational interests and divergent policy framings often clash (Schmidt, 2020).This article considers the European energy crisis as a case study for analysing the Commission's role in a specific institutional and geographical environment. It consists of an interpretative approach to the Commission's role during the crisis and its impact on strengthening the European energy scale. It is based on EU legislation and official documentation, a dozen semi-structured interviews with officials from the Directorate-General for Energy conducted between December 2023 and February 2024, and three months of participant observation between March and June 2023 within the same directorate.This article finds that, despite opposition from certain states, particularly in Eastern Europe, which advocate a national approach to energy policies, the Commission has mostly succeeded in making the European scale the main scale for European energy policies in response to the crisis. This development should be seen in the context of a strengthening of the European scale in the energy field, recently through the regulation on energy governance in the Union. The response to the energy crisis has contributed to this process, in particular through the adoption of joint procurement AggregateEU and the acceleration of the deployment of energy from renewable sources.

title: « Tout a commencé un soir de tempête. » Chroniques géolégales du contentieux énergétique sur l’île de Sein
abstract: This article presents a geolegal analysis of a unique energy transition controversy on Sein island in French Brittany, centred on the first-ever rejection of the traditional electricity distribution system in order to propel a faster transition to renewable sources. In 2013, a citizen-owned company challenged the monopoly of the historical operator of the island's electricity concession to end the island's dependence on oil after repeated but unsuccessful requests to the operator since the 1990s. The island of Sein, located off the coast of Finistère, is a non-interconnected zone, which justifies that a single company has an integrated monopoly on energy supply. The citizen-led company sought not only to generate renewable energy but also to secure access to the grid to manage the balance between supply and demand – a crucial challenge given the intermittent nature of renewable energy. Following a refusal from the historical company, tensions escalated and eventually led to an unprecedented legal dispute. The case, which extended far beyond the island's small territory, took on national and European political significance. The dispute became a subversive act, challenging established political and energy models and forcing a renegotiation of powers over the distribution network. The article addresses two questions: how can the scope and intensity of the dispute be explained, and in what ways does law operate as an instrument of power in the implementation of the energy transition? To answer these questions, it builds on a dual theoretical framework that brings the geolegal literature into dialogue with material politics. In doing so, the article contributes to expanding geolegal scholarship toward socio-technical issues such as energy, while also reflecting on how recent geolegal developments invite a renewed and deepened interrogation of law within political geography. Drawing on a fieldwork conducted in the summer of 2024 (comprising 9 interviews and a week of non-participant observation), this paper explores three central tensions in the construction of energy spatialities. First, it argues that the material characteristics of decentralised, intermittent energy reshape strategic control points within energy systems, positioning the shared distribution network and the related balancing of supply and demand as a central site of power struggles - an issue largely unexplored by geographers. Second, the paper highlights the importance of studying the legal frameworks that give rise to new power hierarchies between actors. Finally, from an energy justice perspective, the case calls into question the legitimacy of vertically integrated monopolies and the resistances to centralised governance. The study shows how law and jurisdictional scales become tools for shaping local resistance. By using European law, local actors challenge historically dominant structures. Beyond the French case, Sein Island highlights the strategic nature of multi-scalar energy governance. This complex interplay of interests reveals the power relations that shape the dynamics of energy transitions across Europe and the trade-offs that can emerge from them. The case is particularly significant as it provides a rare example of a major political and regulatory resistance to electrical decentralization. It contributes to debates on energy justice and the transformation of socio-spatial power relations in the transition, while also providing insights into seizing the growing role of law in energy dynamics within political geography.

title: Le pouvoir des gestionnaires de réseau électrique de gouverner les systèmes électriques insulaires
abstract: At the core of organizational models of island electricity systems - traditionally based on the centralization of power flows (Coutard, Rutherford, 2009) - lies the grid operator, which is legally required to continuously meet consumer demand by regulating electricity generation (Pilo, 2022). Over the past two decades however, the development of decentralized generation technologies (such as solar photovoltaics and wind power), along with advances in energy storage (including batteries and hydrogen), has challenged this centralized organization and, more broadly, the role of grid operators in electricity governance. By bridging the sociology of translation and the sociology of public action, this article contributes to the analysis of the conditions under which sociotechnical systems exhibit “obduracy” (Hommels, 2005) in the face of the hybridization of electricity services (Furlong, 2014; Lawhon et al., 2018; Jaglin, 2019; Pilo, 2022). The analysis draws on a comparative study of Guadeloupe and Barbados - two non-interconnected island electricity systems in which operators combine generation and distribution functions. It is based on two empirical fieldworks comprising 118 semi-structured interviews with a wide range of stakeholders (grid operators, public authorities, regulators, producers, project developers, users, trade unions, and civil society actors), complemented by the analysis of grey literature and regulatory documents, as well as observation sequences capturing governance processes in practice. The findings highlight three main contributions. First, the article shows that the expansion of renewable energy leads to differentiated trajectories depending on sociopolitical contexts: it may result in forms of system reconfiguration - as in Barbados, where decentralized initiatives are integrated into the grid - or in processes of system rigidification, as illustrated by the conversion of thermal power plants in Guadeloupe. Second, despite these variations, the article shows that the interdependence between actors makes the evolution of electricity systems particularly difficult, especially with regard to centralized transmission infrastructures. This dynamic contributes to a form of “obduracy” of sociotechnical systems (Hommels, 2005), as historically dominant grid operators are able to mobilize significant power resources (Lambelet, Pflieger, 2016) through processes of translation (Callon, 1986). Third, the article highlights the reliance of network operators on multidimensional risk regulation instruments, whose importance is heightened in small, autonomous island systems, thereby revealing the significance of the “material fragility” (Denis, Pontille, 2023) of insular infrastructures.

title: Pour une géographie politique des espaces fiscaux du nucléaire : une comparaison entre France et États-Unis
abstract: Local tax revenues generated by energy infrastructures and particularly nuclear power plants are frequently portrayed in the literature as mechanisms of economic dependence that lock host communities into path-dependent trajectories, thus hindering energy transitions. Within energy geography and nuclear studies, these fiscal flows are often implicitly treated as instruments of power benefiting operators by securing local acceptability. This article challenges this assumption by repositioning local nuclear taxation within the field of fiscal geography and by explicitly theorizing power relations. Building on Barnett and Duvall’s multidimensional taxonomy of power, the paper asks whether and how fiscal flows associated with nuclear facilities produce coercive, institutional, structural, or productive power over host territories.Empirically, the article develops a comparative analysis of two nuclear power stations embedded in contrasting fiscal and governance systems, Fessenheim in France and Seabrook in the United States. Methodologically, it proposes a two-step approach. First, it reconstructs the “fiscal spaces” generated by each plant by contextualizing relevant monetary flows, including taxes, subsidies, infrastructure investments, and indirect financial contributions. This reconstruction combines quantitative data (local and intermunicipal public accounts, fiscal reports, impact studies) with qualitative material (semi-structured interviews, grey literature, municipal council records, and field observations). Second, these fiscal spaces are analyzed through Barnett and Duvall’s fourfold framework to identify the concrete modalities through which power is exercised in these flows.The results demonstrate that fiscal flows do not generate uniform or automatic dependencies. In Fessenheim, despite high local revenues linked to nuclear taxation, the operator’s coercive and institutional power over local authorities remains limited, as fiscal rules are centrally defined by the state. Power relations are instead shaped by intermunicipal redistribution mechanisms and national compensation schemes, which produce territorial tensions and shifting positions among local actors. In Seabrook, fiscal relations are negotiated locally through property tax assessments, introducing uncertainty and periodic conflict, but also constraining unilateral domination by either the operator or the municipality. Across both cases, productive power operates unevenly through fiscal imaginaries, strongly in France and weakly in the U.S., reflecting differences in operator status and governance scales. By demonstrating that the political effects of fiscal flows depend on legal frameworks, temporalities, scales, and imaginaries, this article argues for moving beyond reductive notions of addictive economies. It shows that understanding energy transitions requires analyzing money not as an intrinsic source of power, but as a relational and spatialized mediator embedded in specific fiscal spaces

title: Le conflit du parc éolien de Fosen Vind en Norvège : interprétations antagonistes des territoires et de la transition énergétique
abstract: This article examines the conflict sparked by the development of the Fosen Vind mega-wind farm in Norway on grazing lands used by Sámi populations, the only officially recognized indigenous people in mainland Europe. This conflict has been extensively studied by Norwegian researchers, primarily through the prism of political science, law, postcolonial studies or social psychology. Most of the work on the Fosen Vind conflict uses the concepts of ‘energy transition’ and ‘just transition’ to frame the issue, but with little consideration of how these concepts are used by the various actors involved. We will seek to examine the extent to which competing representations of energy transition clash, adopting a reflexive stance on this polysemic concept, which should not only be seen as an analytical framework, but also as a discursive and political construct. We will analyse this conflict through the prism of the cognitive frameworks employed by the actors involved. We will highlight the territorial dimension of this framework, which mobilises different types of relationships with territories, from living spaces closely linked to identity to global spaces.The article is based on a qualitative methodology. This study draws on a month-long period of fieldwork in Norway carried out by one of the authors in March 2022, which included 14 semi-structured individual interviews with various stakeholders (researchers, members of associations campaigning against wind farm development, associations for the protection of indigenous peoples, residents living near wind farms). Encountering some reticence among the Sámi stakeholders to talk about their long and arduous struggle against several wind farms, we focused on informal discussions and participation in the Sámi Easter festival rather than interviews. This fieldwork was complemented by a discourse analysis based on press articles, official government documents, company reports, and NGO publications. Drawing on several field visits carried out between October 2021 and May 2025 by the other author as well as a detailed analysis of Statkraft's annual reports between 2009 and 2025, the cognitive frameworks used by the project's supporters were brought to light. While it is possible to simplify the issue by dividing the actors into two camps, those opposed to Fosen Vind and those in favour of it, an examination of their motivations and representations reveals very different cognitive frameworks, which interact and evolve throughout the conflict. The territoriality of these different frameworks varies: while the Sámi opponents are defending their traditional territories, which have strong cultural, symbolic and identity value, and some residents are seeking to preserve their residential and recreational areas, certain environmental associations are defending ‘nature’ and its biodiversity, or even the national territory, while more generalist discourses on the climate context and environmental protection refer to global issues. While the concept of energy transition is initially little used by the actors involved, the conflict has given rise to discourse on energy transition and has also helped to structure its definition.

title: Recursos renovables y minerales, para demandas externas o necesidades locales. Dos fuerzas de la transición energética argentina
abstract: At the beginning of the 21st century, the transition to a low-carbon energy model, with its opportunities and tensions, modifies the role of fossil fuels in the socio-productive organisation of territories and their hegemony on the global geopolitical scene. The incorporation of peripheral geographies into the global economy through the advancement of new activities and the application of innovative technologies shows the spatial dimension of the transition process (Guibert et al., 2018; Schweitzer, 2016). In Latin America, since the late 20th century, processes have been underway that integrate territories into the international market, with a particular focus on their energy resources. In this region, Argentina—given its availability of land, water, energy, minerals, and other resources—is valued within global accumulation circuits, attracting investment (Vázquez, 2021). Certain regions are valorized by projects that seek to extract strategic minerals, such as lithium, generate electricity and/or produce green hydrogen, taking advantage of available solar and wind resources. The expansion of these energies and the spatial transformations that result from them invite us to rediscover aspects of the relationship between energy and territory. This paper draws on transition studies and energy-territory nexus theories (Bridge and Gailing, 2020; Exner et al., 2015; Hurd et al., 2012; Rothkopf, 2009) to study the energy transition in Argentina from the perspective of the harnessing of strategic renewable and mineral resources, analyzing their contribution to local needs or extraterritorial demands. The paper stems from results of doctoral and postdoctoral research carried out between 2018 and 2025. The research is based on a qualitative methodology and a territorial, multidimensional, and multi-scalar perspective. Initially, documentary analysis was used, including a study of official public documents, a review of national and provincial regulations, and of national and international literature specializing in energy transitions and energy geography. For primary data collection, fieldwork sessions were organized within the framework of collective, interdisciplinary research projects. These sessions involved gathering primary information through on-site observation and semi-structured interviews with key informants at different levels of involvement in the region's energy dynamics. These included managers and technical staff from renewable energy project development companies, investors, electricity distribution companies and cooperatives, public administration officials, civil society actors, non-governmental organizations, and citizens in general. The interviews were structured to identify existing projects, those promoting them, and their objectives. Five main thematic areas were considered to guide the conversation: the genesis and motivation of the initiative; project ownership and financing; actors and stakeholders involved in the project's design and implementation; citizen and local stakeholder involvement; and the intended use of the project's benefits. As part of the main findings, the papers shows that the energy transition in Argentina is driven by two types of processes: one guided by external interests that mobilise resources abroad, exerting a kind of centrifugal force, which serves global value chains and reinforces the country's vocation to satisfy extraterritorial demands; and another, with a centripetal tendency, which emerges from endogenous forces from the territories themselves, seeking to satisfy local needs.

title: « Cultiver » les panneaux solaires : reconfiguration des stratégies d’appropriation foncière dans la transition énergétique colombienne
abstract: In Colombia, the energy transition implemented since the signing of the Paris Agreement (2015) is reconfiguring the geography of electricity production from renewable energy technologies. This article looks at the installation of industrial solar photovoltaic parks and shows how, by becoming part of the country's existing energy networks, they also enable companies to open up new energy fronts. This process is achieved not only by redefining company-state relations, but also by bringing new private players into the energy market. Drawing on analyses from political ecology, the article shows how the installation of solar panels in the context of the energy transition is ultimately a way of reproducing the logics of land appropriation by large energy companies. However, the article analyzes the opening of new energy fronts not through conflict, but rather by attempting to understand how the energy transition can be sustained across territories. I study the conditions for the implementation of photovoltaic solar panel park infrastructure: which actors contribute to promoting the installation of projects, and what governance, social and political relationships are mobilized.This article is based on several months' fieldwork carried out in Colombia between 2022 and 2024, in several regions: Magdalena medio, Caribean coast and Huila departement. More than 30 interviews, participant observation and a review of governmental and entrepreneurial grey literature (legal documents, company reports, press, social networks) were conducted. In addition, the methodology is based on a cartographic analysis using data from Acolgen, the union of electricity producers in Colombia. This data has been spatialized, enabling me to carry out a cartographic analysis of the opening of new fronts. The results are the followings: new energy fronts are being opened up by solar photovoltaic parks through entrepreneurial projects led by large electricity production companies in Colombia. These companies benefit from favorable legislation and tax advantages granted by the Colombian government. In addition, the government strongly encourages the development of photovoltaic parks. Furthermore, companies rely on the support of cattle ranchers who make their land available for electricity production. As the largest landowners in the region, ranchers are seizing the economic opportunity presented by the energy transition and are taking three types of action: they are selling or leasing their land to companies for the construction of solar farms, or they are partnering with them. It would appear that solar projects are meeting with relatively little opposition from the rest of the population, even though the benefits of the transition are not being widely shared. This is because the region where the farms are being built is historically prone to violence and has been subject to harsh repression in the past. Furthermore, the farms do not cause the direct displacement of residents, which seems to explain the absence of open opposition. However, these farms do not appear to contribute to improving energy justice, as the population does not seem to benefit from better electricity service.

title: Approaching the spatial dimensions of environmental justice in adaptation policy. The study of flood risk management
abstract: The risk of flooding is increasing as a result of climate change. The unequal social and spatial impact of flooding poses a significant challenge to flood risk management (FRM) policies and raises concerns about environmental justice. This article contributes to the theoretical justice framework by conducting an empirical analysis of FRM policies in four European countries. Drawing on environmental justice literature as well as the framework of FRM strategies, the article demonstrates that fully incorporating spatial justice into FRM is challenging due to the way in which space is framed and narrated. FRM remains dominated by the concept of fixed and hazard-dependent space. The results highlight three dimensions of spatial justice that are often overlooked. Firstly, there is the temporal dimension, referring to the unequal effects that decisions may have on future generations. Secondly, the relational dimension of space refers to the role of social distance from public policy in determining public participation in decision-making processes. Thirdly, the symbolic dimension refers to space as a narrative construction of identity that shapes spatial practices.
publisher: Société Royale Belge de Géographie and the Belgian National Committee of Geography

title: Robinsonnades noires. Des îles de terreur, survivals extrêmes et isolats postapocalyptiques
abstract: The text examines the transformation of the Robinsonade from its founding myth in Robinson Crusoe to contemporary “dark Robinsonades”. While nineteenth-century narratives promoted rational mastery of nature, survival, and colonial ideology, modern fictions dismantle this imaginary. In a fully known and hostile world, the island is no longer a utopian space but a site of violence, failure, and regression. Contemporary survival stories emphasize the collapse of adaptation, social bonds, and moral frameworks under conditions of scarcity and fear. The island becomes a generalized metaphor for any constraining environment, exposing human vulnerability when confronted with an indifferent or catastrophic world.

title: Le Cratère de James Fenimore Cooper. De la robinsonnade à l’utopie
abstract: The Crater (1847) by James Fenimore Cooper is a political and moral work that combines Robinsonade, utopia, and dystopia. Set against the backdrop of American territorial expansion, the novel follows Mark Woolston, shipwrecked on a barren reef that he makes fertile through labor and scientific knowledge, a metaphor for the conquest of the American frontier. He later establishes an ideal, hierarchical, and conservative society based on property and moral order. However, the influx of settlers, demagoguery, and the corruption of religion, law, and the press lead to the collapse of the utopia, ultimately destroyed by a natural cataclysm, illustrating a pessimistic and cyclical vision of history. In this article, we will seek to show how the successive transitions from Robinson Crusoe to utopia, then from utopia to dystopia, shed light on the political interpretation of Cooper’s work.

title: Des Lumières chrétiennes ?
abstract: This paper reviews Simon Pietro Calisti’s 2025 book on Voltaire’s Anti-Pascal and its eighteenth-century reception. Calisti treats the Anti-Pascal not as scattered marginalia on Pascal’s Pensées but as the polemical core of a long conflict on the nature of “modernity”: a Voltairian, empiricist and anti-Cartesian naturalisation of the human condition, versus a “Christian modernity” defended by theologians and apologetes who mobilise Cartesian and Malebranchian arguments to reconcile reason and faith. The article highlights Calisti’s analysis of the three waves of Voltaire’s Remarques (1734, 1742 and 1778), the central themes of the quarrel (anthropology, Scripture, deism, Deus absconditus), and the decisive role of the Port-Royal editorial tradition, whose partial cartesianisation of Pascal offers rationalist aguments in favour of the Christian faith. The article then questions the contemporary relevance Calisti assigns to Voltaire’s opponents. Stressing Pascal’s own anti-Cartesian, Gassendist epistemology and the crisis of figurist exegesis after Spinoza and Richard Simon, it argues that eighteenth-century apologetes defend Pascal by abandoning Pascal—either sliding toward deism via metaphysical proofs, toward obscurantist mystery, or toward problematic theological guarantees of certainty. A final regret is Calisti’s omission of Pierre Bayle, whose analyses sharpen the apologetic dilemma and complicate any appeal to “Christian Enlightenment”.

title: Dessine-moi une île déserte. Ou la fascination pour la robinsonnade du point de vue de l’intermédialité
abstract: This article examines the enduring fascination with desert islands and the Robinsonade myth from an intermedial perspective. The island, both an imaginary space, an experimental setting, and a symbol of isolation, has crossed centuries and media since Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe. The author analyzes various forms of representation: early maps, poetic atlases blending fact and fiction, historical narratives about real islands, comics (Philémon), and digital devices like the screen saver Johnny Castaway. These examples show how the island gradually becomes a simplified visual formula while retaining strong evocative power. Robinson thus becomes less a character than a narrative principle, constantly adapted and reinterpreted in different cultural and media contexts. The Robinsonade emerges as a fundamental form of fiction, revealing modern imaginaries and their circulation between media.

title: Les robinsonnades. Exploration d’un mythe moderne
abstract: This dossier analyzes robinsonades from Defoe to the present day as a literary, ideological, and media device. After establishing a fiction focused on the individual, the economy, and colonization, the genre was turned on its head by dark robinsonades, then reconfigured through intermediality, which renewed its forms and critical issues.

title: Robinsonnades et philosophie au XVIIIe siècle
abstract: This text examines the Robinsonade in the eighteenth century through Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe, connecting it to Enlightenment debates in philosophy, science, and ideology. Paolo Quintili shows that the early novel emerges at a moment when the boundary between fact and fiction is deeply unstable, both in literature and experimental science, as illustrated by the parallel positions of Defoe and Newton concerning the rejection of feigned hypotheses. The Robinsonade thus presents itself as a fiction claiming moral and cognitive truth and also functions as a thought experiment about the state of nature, social isolation, and individual formation, particularly in Rousseau. At the same time, it conveys a bourgeois ideology, which legitimizes individual labor, property, colonization, and slavery, especially through the relationship between Robinson and Friday. The text highlights the fundamental ambiguity of the Robinsonade, oscillating between moral critique and ideological justification.

title: Alain Lhomme, Le style des philosophes. Pour une approche stylistique des textes philosophiques
Liste des thèses et des habilitations à diriger des recherches (HDR) en anthropologie soutenues en 2025
venue_name: Bulletins et Mémoires de la Société d’Anthropologie de Paris, Vol 38 (2026)

title: Bilateral asymmetry in the lower limbs in medieval humans and La Ferrassie Neandertals LF1 and LF2
abstract: Bilateral asymmetry in the lower limbs can provide insights into habitual biomechanical loading and mobility patterns in past populations. Previous studies have typically examined lower-limb elements in isolation, potentially overlooking integrated functional signals across the entire limb. Here, we present new data on bilateral asymmetry in medieval humans and the La Ferrassie Neandertals (LF1 and LF2), combining external measurements with cross-sectional biomechanical analyses. We quantified directional (DA) and absolute asymmetry (AA) in femora, tibiae and the first (MT1) and fifth metatarsals (MT5) to evaluate habitual mechanical loading. Medieval humans showed moderate asymmetry in MT1 and the tibia, but no consistent side dominance or inter-element correlations, suggesting substantial individual variation. LF1 and LF2 exhibited higher DA, with distinct patterns between individuals, most likely reflecting adaptation to more intense or repetitive lower-limb loading. Overall, our results highlight individual variability, possible sexual dimorphism and segment-specific adaptation, while underscoring that metatarsal asymmetry in past populations has not been well documented to date. In addition, thanks to high-resolution CT data for LF1 and LF2, our study produced revised and more precise estimates of their biomechanical properties.
venue_name: Bulletins et Mémoires de la Société d’Anthropologie de Paris, Vol 38 (2026)

title: Les caprices de Pascal
abstract: Caprice, in the course of the seventeenth century, established itself as a complex and contested term in seventeenth-century French culture and society. The dictionary makers of the period distinguish between positive and negative meanings of the word. Furetière is typical in perceiving the word to have a negative meaning when it is applied to social behaviour that goes against all reasonable norms and in portraying caprice as potentially positive in its meaning when it is used to describe the flash of wit (génie) at the heart of artistic creativity. Louis Marin, in an important 1983 study of the concept, suggests that Pascal is the thinker of the period who articulates the transformation of caprice from a disorder of the imagination to a flash of creative wit. Yet – as this article shows – Pascal nowhere uses the term in that second, positive, sense. How is that absence best understood? As a random lexical effect or as the expression of a rhetorical strategy? In pursuit of the latter hypothesis, the article turns to Marin’s idea that Pascalian discourse produces a certain form of incompletion, using this idea to read anew the lexical presences and absences of caprice in the fabric of Pascal’s writings.
publisher: Groupe de Recherches Interdisciplinaires sur l'Histoire du Littéraire
concepts: Social history and conditions. Social problems. Social reform

title: L’éloge de l’esprit au service des « héroïques qualités » dans la Lettre à la reine Christine de Suède
abstract: My article is about the « heroic qualities » that Pascal attributes to the queen Christina of Sweden at the end of the eulogy which he writes for her when he sends her the mechanical calculator. In so doing, my research aims to understand the connection between the « heroic qualities » and the « heroic virtues », which at the time were more commonly used, but which could have hardly been given to Christina, since she was a woman and a Protestant. Therefore, my analysis will seek to prove that Pascal shifts the scope of the eulogy of the Swedish princess from the moral to the intellectual excellence.
publisher: Groupe de Recherches Interdisciplinaires sur l'Histoire du Littéraire
concepts: Social history and conditions. Social problems. Social reform

title: Publishing in the Social and Human Sciences in the Age of Globalization and Digital Technology
The Americanization of the French Social and Human Sciences? A Cartography of Translations from English, German, and Italian into French (2003–2013)
abstract: Translating books is more significant for the international circulation of ideas within the social and human sciences than it is within the sciences. However, chances of a book being translated vary according to various factors: the centrality of original language, the symbolic capital of the author, and that of their publisher. This study of works in the social and human sciences translated into French between 2003 and 2013 reveals the state of unequal power relations between the three languages from which most of them originate: English, German, and Italian. The study shows that although the German tradition is still valued in the sub-field of the human and social sciences publishing in France, we are witnessing the virtual disappearance of contemporary German authors in favor of British and American researchers. This finding tends to confirm the idea of an American hegemony, which however needs to be relativized. The study of the authors of prefaces also reveals the different importation strategies of the cultural intermediaries (editors, literary agents) in this sub-field: economic, political, symbolic and academic.

title: French Social Sciences Journals: Disciplines and Editorial Practices
abstract: This article analyses the structure and the transformations within the landscape of French SSH academic journals. It relies on a database listing more than 200 French journals classified by the academic research evaluation agency AÉRES (Agence d’évaluation de la recherche et de l’enseignement supérieur) at the beginning of 2010s within six fields: economics and management; sociology and demography; political science; anthropology; psychology; philosophy. First, this article highlights the high level of dispersion in the editorial landscape (characterized by a multiplicity of small and not-for-profits actors), its variation from one discipline to another (in a way that echoes the conflict of the faculties) and the concentration of the industry, monopolized by a few major publishers. Second, it focuses on issues to do with digitalization and institutional politics in favour of open access, which since the 2010s have had an impact on the forms of distribution of journals in a period marked by the emergence of platforms such as Cairn and OpenEdition. This article shows that these changes have occurred without breaking with traditional ways of publishing SSH and have not (yet) produced a genuine upheaval of journals ecosystem.

title: Negotiating the Boundaries of the Speakable: The Introduction of Western Social and Human Sciences into the USSR by Progress Publishers (1963-1985)
abstract: This paper examines the circulation of ideas and knowledge between Western countries and the Soviet Union through the translation of books in the social and human sciences. The analysis focuses on the activity of Progress Publishers (1963-1996), a Soviet publishing house with a privileged status and a dual mission: to promote the classic works of Marxism-Leninism and the scholarly output of Soviet specialists abroad; and to publish translations of “bourgeois” Western thought and distribute them in the USSR. As a state-run publisher, subject to the control of censors and government bodies, Progress manoeuvred between ideological constraints, state demands, and scientific interests, and this was reflected in its position at the intersection of the political, academic, and publishing fields. This study highlights the key role played by Progress in the introduction of new ideas in the social and human sciences into the USSR between the 1960s and 1980s. By analysing its internal structure and the socio-occupational trajectories of publishing managers, and reconstructing the academic networks associated with the publisher and its catalogues, this article reveals the logics that determined which books were imported, and examines the constraints on the production of translations in an authoritarian context.

title: Another Break in the Wall
abstract: Borders, walls, and migrant characters who challenge them feature prominently in the works of Hugo Hamilton, a transnational author whose German mother immigrated to Ireland after World War 2. This article focuses on the depiction of the Berlin Wall in four of his novels set in Germany. Interweaving personal and world histories, past and present, Hamilton explores relationships – with places as much as with people. In Surrogate City (1990), the narrative focuses on the character of Helen who has moved from Ireland to West Berlin, while the characters in The Love Test (1995) are from East Berlin and attempt to cross over to flee the Stasi. The protagonist of Disguise (2008) is in and out of Berlin in search of his own story and history. In Every Single Minute (2014), the narrator Liam takes his dying friend on a last touristic trip to the German capital. The corpus offers four different perspectives on the Berlin Wall that span a little over a decade in terms of publication, but nearly forty years with regards to the narratives: Surrogate City is set during the Cold War, The Love Test and Disguise alternate between chapters in a post-war, partitioned Germany and passages set in the aftermath of 1989, while Every Single Minute takes place in contemporary times. This study focuses on the depiction and significance of the Berlin Wall in the novels, from its historical role as a boundary between two worldviews, separating people, to its fall and the aftermath of it. The chronology of the novels reflects that of the Wall’s history and affects its depiction in the narratives. This geocritical study examines the fictional representation of a geographical place and the evolution of this portrayal. Simultaneously, the article argues for the use of sensorial mapping in literary analysis. Exemplifying it through the study of Hamilton’s novels, a case is made for this cartographical practice that subverts the conventions of the discipline in order to highlight emotions and impressions, making it all the more suited to literary geography and geocriticism. Maps are thus included to illustrate and reinforce the points made in this study, further challenging the boundaries between disciplines.

title: Introduction
Anomalous Borders, Geographical Knowledge, and the Inner Line in India
abstract: This article examines the Inner Line system in British India’s northeastern frontier to show how borders are historically produced and dynamic. Introduced through the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation of 1873, the Inner Line operated as an internal administrative partition that nonetheless functioned as the practical limit of sovereign authority in a region where the external border remained undefined until 1914. What existed beyond the Inner Line, therefore, was a zone where sovereignty was fragmented and where law remained mired in ambiguity.Over time, the Inner Line was repeatedly redefined, becoming a key element of colonial governance in the region – all the while remaining indefinite, almost by design. It enabled extra-legal colonial interventions and institutionalised a civilizational distinction between the hill and valley populations. The article traces various spatial and ethnological discourses that framed the hills as an unruly frontier. This representation underpinned the Inner Line and was developed over the 19th and 20th centuries through surveying, mapping and ethnological classification to naturalise a new colonial territorial order. It argues that the line was not just a geographical division but a mechanism that reshaped the region’s patterns of mobility and association to fit within the imperial economic and administrative order. Previous studies on northeastern India have analysed how colonial interventions framed the region’s geography, agrarian structure, and security concerns. This article builds on such scholarship, situating the Inner Line within wider discussions on frontiers in British India. By tracing how the Line was repeatedly redrawn, amended, and circumvented, the article emphasises its fluidity and its role as a flexible technology of power that regulated mobility, economic extraction, and administrative reach. Finally, I show how, in post‑colonial India, the Inner Line has acquired new and often competing meanings — becoming at once a security instrument, a mechanism of indigenous protection, and a site of political contestation.

title: Ghost borders: Mapping the Disappearing Strasbourg-Kehl Borderlands
Dynamic borderscapes and creative countermappings in Shubhangi Swarup’s Latitudes of Longing (2018)
abstract: This paper employs the concept of the borderscape to analyse Shubhangi Swarup’s novel Latitudes of Longing (2018) which is set in various border regions of the Indian nation. I argue that the prism of the borderscape enables an analysis of India’s borders as dynamic and complex spaces from which counter-hegemonic cartographies of the nation-state can emerge. Through the multiple and trans-scalar perspectives of the borderscape, these new mappings delink from the modern narrative of “singular and secular time” (Chakrabarty 2000: 16) as well as gendered distributions of space that perpetuate colonial and nationalist power relations. The resulting counter-cartography draws attention to human flows of mobility and the constant natural transformations of the territory by natural forces such as earthquakes. This shifts the attention away from efforts to securitise natural borders and instead exposes their potential for fostering solidarity between nations as well generating more inclusive visions of national belonging.

title: Interruption and Solace: Medicine Lines in Louise Erdrich’s The Sentence (2021)
abstract: This paper examines North American Métis heritage from a resurgent and decolonial perspective. Erdrich’s novel is set in the Western borderland of the Red River Valley where Europeans, and Ojibwe, Cree, and Métis peoples intermingled and created enduring kinship relations that favor transcultural exchanges. Those relations are maintained thanks to the resurgence of Métis relationality. The novel offers new syncretic imaginings like the Rougarou that threatens but eventually maintains Métis traditions. Tookie eventually achieves solace despite colonial attempts at erasure and reconfigures her own perception of loss. She becomes an agent of co-resistance and questions the legitimacy of colonial power as she embraces the fight for social justice. As Minneapolis struggles against the impacts of COVID-19 and colonial violence, Tookie re-maps and rewrites Métis peoplehood across the Canada-U.S. border.

title: On the Borders of the Imaginary, “Erring” on the Side of Hope: Western Mapping, Exploration and the Jeffersonian Design
abstract: Christopher Columbus and James Cook both share similar features—one of them is to have failed to discover what made up the actual purpose of their quests; they did, however, “f[i]nd what they wanted to see,” as reflected in the writings and maps the two illustrious explorers handed over to posterity. This assumption by Thomas P. Slaughter appears to also fully apply to Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, sent by Thomas Jefferson beyond the frontier, in search of the legendary Northwest Passage, a hypothetical transcontinental water route the control of which would promote the implementation of the expansionist design. While the enterprise itself—among other objectives—aimed at furthering cartographic knowledge, the prospect of exploration also required to be fully acquainted with the region to be traveled, ahead of the journey. Jefferson had succeeded in gathering precious data but the mental image still remained very much incomplete: his judgment was flawed with regard to the actual distances and hardships of the project, which might never have taken shape, had the fictitious map not temporarily supplanted the true reality of frontier geography. Challenged throughout the “wilderness” experience, the heralds of Jeffersonianism quickly measured the gap between the mental construct and actual daily life within an unconquerable natural environment that put the Western cartographers under heavy strain, even undermining their methodology. The travelers also took particular care in collecting the invaluable information provided by the Natives—whose perfect mastery of the territory had been granted to them by the thousands of years during which they had been occupying the place—only to find out that the Native American approach to cartography usually mirrors Indigenous thinking more than it helps deepen the “civilized” man’s understanding of the spatio-temporal framework he progresses in. In this respect, beside merely representing space, maps might also be construed as the subjective projection of the mind they spring from.

title: How Donald Trump’s intentional mispronunciations of Kamala Harris’s first name support the hypothesis that loanwords exhibit distinct phonological properties
abstract: This study shows how Donald Trump, by intentionally mispronouncing the first name of his opponent in the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris, supports the theory that the English lexicon is composed of subsystems. The words which belong to one subsystem share linguistic properties that distinguish them from the items of the other subsystems. Each subsystem arises from the interaction of specific phonetic, phonological, letter-to-sound, morphological, segmental, syntactic, semantic, and frequency-related properties, which makes it possible to distinguish the subsystems from each other. Native English speakers are sensitive to the different properties of sublexica and in particular to those of loanwords which are grouped in the §Foreign subsystem. The words of the §Foreign subsystem balance conforming to English-system principles with maintaining their own distinct features, as they often retain some properties of the source languages. This conflict gives them a specific status in English, especially from the point of view of pronunciation. By intentionally pronouncing Kamala Harris’s first name with phonetic and phonological principles that are typically attested in the words of foreign origin and which are detailed in the article (location of primary stress, pronunciation of stressed vowels with a “foreign value” and absence of vowel reduction in unstressed contexts), Donald Trump, as a political strategist, points to Kamala Harris’s origin and, by doing so, attempts to discredit the Democratic candidate in the eyes of the American electorate.

title: Restoring Wonder: Mystical Counter-Mapping in the Work of Arthur Machen
abstract: The Welsh writer Arthur Machen (1863-1947) is now widely recognized as a literary precursor of psychogeography, both as a way of walking and as a study of the interaction between geography and psychology. Like their creator, many of his characters practise what Machen called “the art of wandering”, an art not unlike the situationist dérive in that it liberates the walker from the alienation of the everyday.This article explores Machen’s London writing, both fictional and non-fictional, to show how it ties in with his mystical agenda as a writer. The author and his fictional mouthpieces consistently voice their dislike of the disenchanted, de-spiritualized world they live in. As they participate in the disenchantment of space, maps and guidebooks are rejected in an explicit anti-map discourse. Furthermore, maps cannot render the porosity of space as perceived by the mystically inclined, for whom gateways into the unknown might appear almost anywhere. I argue that the reshaping of London in Machen’s work is an act of counter-mapping in that it opposes what Peter Ackroyd describes as “a secular view of the world”.

title: A Performative Intermedial Analysis of The Willow Song
abstract: This study offers a performative intermedial analysis of The Willow Song in Shakespeare’s Othello, examining how lyrics and music interact as mutually shaping media and how this multimodal relationship contributes to the play’s emotional, symbolic, and educational resonance. Building on theories of embodied cognition and multimodal learning, the article conceptualises intermedial analysis as an approach that integrates literary and musicological perspectives through the act of performing the song, thereby foregrounding aesthetic, affective, and experiential dimensions often overlooked in strictly textual readings. The Willow Song, introduced in the 1623 Folio version of Othello, emerges as a culturally stratified artefact rooted in Renaissance melancholy traditions, where the willow symbolised sorrow and abandoned love. Its appearance in Act IV, Scene 3—sung by Desdemona in an intimate domestic exchange with Emilia—functions as a lyrical and emotional counterpoint to the brutal logic of toxic masculinity, racial prejudice, and patriarchal violence that drives the tragedy toward its catastrophic end. The article contextualises the song within the broader narrative structure of Othello, exploring themes of racism, xenophobia, and femicide that remain profoundly resonant in contemporary society. Drawing on historical and critical sources, the study traces how Shakespeare reworked earlier narratives to address the contradictions of Elizabethan London—a city characterised by social hierarchy, mercantile expansion, and growing ethnic diversity. The contribution underlines how musicality permeates Shakespeare’s dramaturgy, presenting a detailed intermedial analysis of The Willow Song, based on an archival transcription consulted at the Barbican Centre Music Library. The analysis examines melodic contour, modal inflections, rhetorical figures, prosody, phonetic patterns, and their articulation with lyrical content. Features such as descending fifths, modal shifts between Aeolian, Dorian, and major inflections, repeated motifs, and rhetorical devices like hypotyposis contribute to the song’s haunting emotional effect. The lyrics amplify this musical expressiveness through alliteration, sibilance, consonance, assonance, personification, and symbolic imagery, producing a refined sonic texture that mirrors the play’s thematic concerns. The article concludes by highlighting the educational potential of intermedial approaches to Shakespeare. In a sociocultural context marked by declining engagement with literary classics and increasing educational fragmentation, music-literature laboratories offer valuable opportunities for multimodal and multisensory learning. By integrating performance, analysis, and embodied interpretation, The Willow Song can serve as an entry point for students—particularly non-native speakers—to engage critically with Shakespeare’s texts, fostering inclusive participation and creative inquiry.

title: Claiming Space: Aboriginal (Re)mappings of Contemporary Australia
abstract: Contemporary Indigenous-authored texts are often read as counter-narratives seeking to redress erroneous and oppressive representations of themselves in white-authored texts. Similarly, Indigenous narratives concerned with place and reclaiming the land lost to colonisation can be read as counter-mapping exercises, insofar as they engage not only with representations of space and the territory itself, but also question the very legitimacy of colonial cartography and therefore settler presence and ways of constructing knowledge about place. This paper engages with the Australian Aboriginal notion of “country” and its relationship with language, particularly in Alexis Wright’s 2006 award-winning novel Carpentaria, set in the eponymous Gulf of Carpentaria in far-north Queensland. Carpentaria tells the story of the Aboriginal Pricklebush people and their relationship with Uptown, the white zone of the fictional town of Desperance, and the Gurrfurrit mine. I argue that Wright is concerned with the way language is used in contemporary Australia to (re)inscribe Aboriginal presence onto the land and overwrite colonial inscriptions through the renaming of colonised places, the articulation of spiritual spaces such as the Dreaming, as well as the remapping of Indigenous bodies and languages as textual spaces. Indeed, Aboriginal writing itself can be likened to a frontier zone along which lies, on one side of the border, literacy, theory, materiality, and history; and on the other side, orality, experience, performance, and myth. Beyond stereotypical binaries, Wright writes from this frontier zone that blurs the border between the margin and centre of postcolonial discourse and complicates the position of the white reader in relation to space(s). Drawing from postcolonial theories of language, territory, and embodiment, I examine how Wright addresses the tensions between local traditions and rampant globalisation to illustrate the ongoing struggle for Indigenous mapping systems to overwrite external and internal colonial cartography, from natural features such as rivers in the Gulf, to sacred spaces like the Dreaming, and even the inner landscape of the reader who attempts to situate themselves within the story and orientate themselves with Wright’s words. As a response to colonial cartography, I examine “unsettlement” as particularly apt to describe the contemporary thrust of Aboriginal writing in Australia, where the very legitimacy of the settler state is threatened by official acknowledgements of the illegality of colonisation, as well as previous and ongoing ownership of the land by Indigenous people.

title: Mapping Resistance and Resilience
L’Architecte face à la boîte noire
abstract: This article examines the instrumentation of architectural design processes in the digital age, placing the question of the image and its transformations at the center of the discussion. It is based on the hypothesis that every project originates from a mental image, which the architect seeks to translate into reality through a series of mediations. This translation is not a simple passage from idea to form, but rather a set of transformations operating within black boxes, understood as systems whose inputs and outputs are identifiable, while their internal logics are opaque. Within this framework, the article proposes to move beyond the opposition between traditional drawing and digital imagery by describing design as a dynamic process of circulation and transformation of images. For the architect, the mental image unfolds between a projected image, that which intention manages to formulate, and a perceived image, that which is interpreted in return. From the machine’s perspective, the image is configured between a thought image, that which can effectively be transmitted to a computer, and a visualized thought, that which is made visible on the screen. Design thus appears as a space of negotiation between these four instances, the coherence of which conditions the act of projecting. The introduction of digital tools and computer-generated imagery is not merely a change of medium, but profoundly transforms the very conditions of architectural thinking. These technical devices orient, filter, and shape design gestures, leading to formatting phenomena through which the projected image tends to adjust to the constraints of the thought image; that is, to the translation capacities offered by digital systems. The risk is thus one of homogenization of production, where form follows the implicit logics of the tools. To analyze this reconfiguration, the article proposes a taxonomy of design postures—user, gamer, maker, and hacker—describing different ways of articulating black boxes and the relationships between intention, perception, and generation. This classification highlights a shift in the role of the architect, who can no longer be understood solely as an author, but rather as a mediator within a sociotechnical network composed of both human and non-human actors. Ultimately, the article argues that the contemporary challenge is not to fully eliminate the opacity of these systems, but to develop a technical culture that enables their understanding, manipulation, and appropriation. Only on this basis may architects avoid alienation and reassert a critical capacity in relation to these tools.
venue_name: Les Cahiers de la Recherche Architecturale, Urbaine et Paysagère, Vol 26 (2026)

title: De l’atlas au dataset. Notes sur une imagination architecturale artificielle et étendue
abstract: For architects, collecting and organising images represents a form of externalisation of the process by which their imagination is constructed. This article sets out to explore how AI-generated images may constitute a further evolution of this process. It draws on the extended mind theory developed by philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers, recently updated by Clark to suggest that large language model (LLM)-based AI systems may externalise human cognitive faculties. It examines the extent to which architectural images produced by generative adversarial networks (GAN) and diffusion models—capable of generating new images from large datasets—might contribute to the ecology of the externalisation of architectural imagination. Through the lens of visual culture, the article analyses the types of AI-generated architectural images currently circulating, focusing on case studies from the French context. Two main categories are identified in particular: photorealistic depictions of feasible buildings, and unrealistic or unbuildable ones. It then outlines potential scenarios—both negative and positive—that these two types of images could open up for architectural imagination, considered through the framework of the extended mind.
